title: The deflated Sharpe ratio
objectives: Deflate a Sharpe ratio for the number of trials behind it.
Compute the probabilistic Sharpe ratio with skew and kurtosis.

screens.title: The best of ten
screens.prose: A researcher backtests 10 strategy variants over 3 years and reports the best, with a Sharpe ratio of 1.5. Suppose every variant is noise: true Sharpe 0. Each run below is one such search of 10, scored by whether its best reaches 1.5.
screens.question: Run at least 1,000 searches. What share of them find a best Sharpe of 1.5 or more?

widget.label: Share of searches
widget.accept: any value from 0.034 to 0.058. The exact share is $1 - \Phi(1.5\sqrt3)^{10} = 0.046$.

hints.text: Press Run 1,000 and read the first bar.
The first bar is the share of searches whose best reached 1.5.
It settles near 0.05: about 1 search in 22.

feedback.correct: About 1 search in 22 finds a 1.5 from pure noise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run 1,000 searches and read the height of the first bar.

byKey.one: That is about the chance for one variant. The best of 10 has ten chances.
byKey.all: Most searches stay below 1.5; read the first bar, not the second.

explain.text: About 4.6% of noise searches report 1.5 or more: a single strategy would do it only 0.5% of the time. The testing course (Is this Sharpe ratio real?) found the same effect for the best of 100. This lesson turns it into a number you can quote.

screens.title: The probabilistic Sharpe ratio
screens.prose: Work per day: a Sharpe of 1.5 a year is $1.5/\sqrt{252} = 0.0945$ a day, over $n = 756$ days. Bailey and López de Prado (2014; AFML chapter 14) give its standard error, with skew $\gamma_3$ and kurtosis $\gamma_4$ (3 for a normal): $$\hat\sigma_{SR} = \sqrt{\frac{1 - \gamma_3 SR + \frac{\gamma_4 - 1}{4}SR^2}{n - 1}}.$$
screens.question: For normal returns ($\gamma_3 = 0$, $\gamma_4 = 3$), what is the standard error? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: With $\gamma_3 = 0$ and $\gamma_4 = 3$ the top is $1 + \tfrac12 SR^2$.

feedback.correct: The daily Sharpe of 0.0945 sits 2.6 standard errors above 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $SR = 0.0945$, $\gamma_3 = 0$, $\gamma_4 = 3$ and $n = 756$ into the formula.

byKey.annual: You used the annual Sharpe 1.5. The formula takes the Sharpe per observation, here per day.
byKey.nosr: Close: that is $1/\sqrt{755}$, which leaves out the $SR^2$ term. Keep it: 0.03647.

explain.text: The standard error is 0.0365, so $z = 0.0945/0.0365 = 2.59$ and $\Phi(2.59) = 0.995$. That is the **probabilistic Sharpe ratio** (PSR): the probability that the true Sharpe beats a benchmark, here 0, $$\text{PSR}(SR^*) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{SR - SR^*}{\hat\sigma_{SR}}\right).$$ The shaded area is it.

screens.title: Same Sharpe, different tails
screens.prose: Three monthly strategies, each with a Sharpe of 0.3 a month (1.04 a year) over $n = 60$ months. Their measured skew and kurtosis differ.
screens.question: Fill in each standard error to 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Negative skew and fat tails both widen the error for the same Sharpe.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $1 - \gamma_3 SR + \tfrac{\gamma_4 - 1}{4}SR^2$ for each row, divide by 59, take the root.

explain.text: Negative skew adds 20% to the standard error and kurtosis 12 adds 9%. A strategy that earns small gains and takes rare big losses looks steadier than it is. The Sharpe alone cannot tell you.

screens.title: Raising the bar to the best of N
screens.prose: If $N$ noise strategies are tried, the best Sharpe is expected near $$E[\max] \approx \sqrt V\left((1 - \gamma)\Phi^{-1}\!\left(1 - \tfrac1N\right) + \gamma\,\Phi^{-1}\!\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{Ne}\right)\right),$$ with $\gamma = 0.5772$ (Euler-Mascheroni) and $V$ the variance of the trials' Sharpes. For noise, $V = 1/(n - 1)$.
screens.question: For $N = 10$ trials over 756 days, what is $E[\max]$ as an annual Sharpe? Give 2 decimal places.

widget.label: Expected best noise Sharpe
widget.accept: 0.91: $\sqrt V = 0.0364$ a day; the bracket is 1.575; $0.0364 \times 1.575 \times \sqrt{252} = 0.91$.

feedback.correct: Ten noise trials over 3 years are expected to show a best Sharpe of 0.91.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work the bracket, multiply by $\sqrt V = 1/\sqrt{755}$, then annualise.

byKey.daily: That is the daily value. Multiply by $\sqrt{252}$ to compare with 1.5.
byKey.rule: That is the rough bound $\sqrt{2\ln N}/\sqrt T$ from the testing course. This formula is closer to the true mean.

explain.text: For $N = 10$ the formula gives 0.91 a year. Check it against a seeded simulation: the testing course's best of 100 over 5 years averaged 1.12 (seed 77), and the formula gives 1.13. It runs about 1% high, close enough for a benchmark.

screens.title: The deflated Sharpe ratio
screens.prose: The **deflated Sharpe ratio** (DSR) is the PSR with the benchmark raised to $E[\max]$ for the $N$ trials: the chance that the reported Sharpe beats the best that noise would show. The curve is DSR against $N$ for our 1.5 over 3 years. Slide $N$.
screens.question: What is the smallest whole number of trials for which the DSR falls below 0.95?

hints.text: Slide $N$ down from 10 and watch the caption.

feedback.correct: Four trials are enough to make a 1.5 over 3 years doubtful.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the curve crosses the 0.95 line, then take the next whole number.

byKey.ten: At 10 trials the DSR is 0.85, well below. It crosses 0.95 much earlier.
byKey.hundred: At 100 trials the DSR is 0.53. It crosses 0.95 at a handful of trials.

explain.text: The DSR drops below 0.95 at $N = 4$. Edge case: at $N = 1$ there is no search, $E[\max] = 0$ and the DSR is the PSR against zero, 0.995. Three years of a 1.5 Sharpe survive only if almost nothing else was tried.

screens.title: The haircut
screens.prose: Another view: how much of the reported 1.5 would noise alone deliver? The bars are $E[\max]$, annualised, for 3 years of daily data.
screens.question: At $N = 100$, what share of the reported Sharpe would noise alone explain? Give a percentage to the nearest whole number.

feedback.correct: After 100 trials, almost all of the 1.5 is what noise would show.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the $N = 100$ bar by the reported 1.5.

byKey.left: That is the share left over. The question asks what noise explains.
byKey.ten: That is the share at $N = 10$. Read the $N = 100$ bar.

explain.text: Noise explains 61% of the 1.5 at $N = 10$, 97% at 100, and more than all of it at 1,000. The haircut grows slowly with $N$, roughly like $\sqrt{2\ln N}$, but it never stops growing.

screens.title: Which trials count?
screens.prose: A note reports three variants of a signal, the best with Sharpe 1.5 over 3 years. The research team's trial log (validation, Trying too many models) shows 60 configurations run on the same data: lookbacks, filters and two models that were dropped.
screens.question: Which DSR should the note report?

options.text: 0.959: only the three reported variants were candidates
options.why: You counted the reported trials. Every configuration that could have been chosen counts, including the dropped ones.

options.text: About 0.78, the average of the two
options.why: There is one right count: the 60 configurations actually tried on this data.

options.text: Neither: the DSR only applies to random strategies
options.why: The DSR applies to any search. It asks whether the best beats what noise would give the best of the same number of tries.

hints.text: Which configurations could have ended up as the reported best?
Any of the 60 runs could have won the search.
Count all 60: the DSR falls from 0.96 to 0.60.

feedback.correct: Every run on the data is a trial, reported or not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The count is every configuration tried, including those not reported.

byKey.three: You counted only the reported trials. The 57 dropped runs were chances to find a lucky best, so they count.

explain.text: The search covered 60 configurations, so the benchmark is the best of 60, 1.35 a year, and the DSR is 0.60: weak evidence. Counting only the three shown gives 0.96. This is why the trial log starts before the first run.

screens.title: Overlapping returns
screens.prose: A researcher scores a signal on 10-day returns sampled every day: 756 observations over 3 years. Neighbouring 10-day returns share 9 days. As in level 1 (Overlapping labels), the effective number of independent observations is about $756/10 \approx 76$.
screens.question: Using $n = 76$ instead of 756, by what factor does the standard error grow? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: The honest standard error is about three times larger.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the square root of the ratio of $n - 1$.

byKey.ten: The error scales with the square root of $n$, so a tenth of the data gives $\sqrt{10}$, not 10.
byKey.ratio: That is the factor by which it shrinks the other way. With fewer observations it grows.

explain.text: Counting overlapping rows as independent makes the standard error about 3.2 times too small. A $z$ of 3 becomes about 1. Use the effective $n$, or non-overlapping returns, in every PSR and DSR.

screens.title: PSR in code
screens.prose: Now in code. `sr` is the Sharpe per observation, `n` the number of observations, `kurt` the full kurtosis (3 for a normal). In SciPy that is `kurtosis(x, fisher=False)`. Use `math.erf` for $\Phi$ and round the PSR to 4 places.
screens.question: Complete `sharpe_se(sr, n, skew, kurt)` and `psr(sr, sr_benchmark, n, skew, kurt)`.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests, including a Sharpe of 0, a benchmark above the Sharpe and one equal to it. Standard errors are rounded to 6 places and PSRs to 4, then compared with math.isclose. Pure Python: nothing to load.

hints.text: The standard error is one line: `math.sqrt((1 - skew * sr + (kurt - 1) / 4 * sr ** 2) / (n - 1))`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the sign of the skew term and that `kurt` is the full kurtosis.

explain.text: The skew term enters with a minus sign, so negative skew raises the error. Passing SciPy's default excess kurtosis (normal 0) would understate the error: always say which kurtosis you mean.

screens.title: DSR in code
screens.prose: Last piece. `expected_max_sharpe` returns 0.0 for a single trial, else the formula, with `statistics.NormalDist().inv_cdf` for $\Phi^{-1}$. `dsr` is the PSR with that benchmark. `psr` from the last screen is defined.
screens.question: Complete `expected_max_sharpe(n_trials, var_trials)` and `dsr(sr, n, skew, kurt, n_trials, var_trials)`.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: expected maxima from 1 to 1,000 trials and five DSRs, one for a single trial. Results are rounded and compared with math.isclose. Pure Python (`statistics` is in the standard library): nothing to load.

hints.text: `dsr` is one line: `psr(sr, expected_max_sharpe(n_trials, var_trials), n, skew, kurt)`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the $Ne$ in the second term and the square root of the variance.

explain.text: For 100 noise trials with $V = 1$ the formula gives 2.531; the exact mean of the best of 100 normals is 2.508. The gap of about 1% is the price of a closed form. With $N = 1$ the DSR equals the PSR against zero.

screens.title: The fund pitch
screens.prose: A fund pitches a Sharpe of 2.1 over 2 years of daily returns, $n = 504$. Due diligence finds it was the best of 40 variants. Daily skew is −0.5 and kurtosis 5. Under noise, $V = 1/503$.
screens.question: What is the deflated Sharpe ratio? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: A DSR of 0.77: suggestive, not convincing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract $E[\max]$ from the daily Sharpe, divide by the standard error, then apply $\Phi$.

byKey.psr: That is the PSR against zero, 0.998. The search of 40 raises the benchmark to $E[\max]$.
byKey.normal: Close: 0.781 is the DSR assuming normal returns. With skew −0.5 and kurtosis 5 the error is a little wider.

explain.text: The PSR against zero is 0.998, but against the best of 40 it is 0.77. The 2.1 is above what noise would give, but not by enough to be sure. A desk records the trial count in every research note so a reader can do this sum.

ideas: The standard error of a Sharpe ratio grows with negative skew and fat tails: $\hat\sigma_{SR} = \sqrt{(1 - \gamma_3 SR + \tfrac{\gamma_4 - 1}{4}SR^2)/(n - 1)}$, per observation.
The PSR is $\Phi((SR - SR^*)/\hat\sigma_{SR})$; the DSR sets $SR^*$ to the expected best of $N$ noise trials.
$N$ is every configuration tried on the data, and $n$ is the effective number of independent observations.
summary.trap: Counting only the reported trials. Every configuration run on the data could have been the winner.

quiz.prose: A pension fund fixed one rule in advance and ran nothing else. Its PSR against zero is 0.97.
quiz.question: What is its DSR?

widget.label: DSR
widget.accept: 0.97: with $N = 1$, $E[\max] = 0$ and the DSR is the PSR against zero.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What is the expected best of a single noise trial?

byKey.zero: With one trial there is no search to correct for.

explain.text: With $N = 1$ the benchmark is the expected Sharpe of one noise strategy, 0. So the DSR equals the PSR against zero, 0.97.

quiz.prose: Two monthly strategies have Sharpe 0.4 a month over 60 months. One has normal returns; the other sells insurance: skew −2, kurtosis 10.
quiz.question: What is the insurance seller's standard error? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $1 - \gamma_3 SR + \tfrac{\gamma_4 - 1}{4}SR^2$ with $\gamma_3 = -2$, $\gamma_4 = 10$.

byKey.normal: That is the normal strategy's error. Negative skew and fat tails widen it.
byKey.signflip: You subtracted the skew term the wrong way. With $\gamma_3 = -2$, $-\gamma_3 SR = +0.8$.

explain.text: The top is $1 + 0.8 + 2.25 \times 0.16 = 2.16$, so the error is $\sqrt{2.16/59} = 0.191$, against 0.135 for normal returns. Rare large losses make a high Sharpe less certain.

quiz.prose: Edge case. A new strategy shows a Sharpe of 0.5 a month (1.73 a year) over 12 months, normal returns, one trial.
quiz.question: Is its PSR against zero above 0.95?

options.text: No: 0.94, because 12 observations give a standard error of 0.32
Yes: an annual Sharpe of 1.73 is always significant
options.why: You judged the Sharpe without its standard error. With $n = 12$ it is $\sqrt{1.0625/11} = 0.31$, so $z = 1.6$.

options.text: The PSR cannot be computed with one trial
options.why: One trial is fine: the PSR needs a Sharpe, $n$, skew and kurtosis.

options.text: Yes, and the DSR is higher still
options.why: The DSR is never above the PSR against zero: the benchmark only rises with $N$.

feedback.correct: A year of data is too short to be sure of almost anything.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the standard error with $n = 12$.

explain.text: The error is $\sqrt{(1 + 0.5 \times 0.25)/11} = 0.32$, so $z = 0.5/0.32 = 1.56$ and PSR $= 0.94$. With too little data, nothing is significant.

quiz.prose: A desk asks every research note to state the number of configurations tried, including the failures.
quiz.question: Why?

options.text: So a reader can set $N$ and deflate the Sharpe
To check the researcher worked hard enough
options.why: Effort is not the point. The count sets the benchmark the best result must beat.
The trial count says nothing about costs. It sets $E[\max]$.

options.text: It changes nothing if the best result is good
options.why: A good best result is exactly what a large search produces by luck. The count tells you how large the search was.

feedback.correct: The count is the $N$ in the DSR.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what $N$ does to the benchmark.

explain.text: Without the count a reader cannot tell a 1.5 from one trial (DSR 0.995) from the best of 100 (0.53). The count is part of the result.
